implementation_notes: Ruby's unfold is the enumerator: Enumerator.produce(seed) { |prev| ... } applies the block to the previous value and yields each result, and raising StopIteration from the block ends the iteration, so the seed-stepping loop becomes a library call. Enumerator.new { |y| ... } is the manual form for steps that must yield several values, run a loop or carry richer state, and chaining .lazy turns either into a lazy pipeline so filter/map/take compose without materialising the sequence. An Enumerator is externally driven, so even without .lazy only the requested elements are produced.
pitfalls: Without StopIteration (or an external take) Enumerator.produce generates forever; laziness alone does not bound it.
Forcing methods (to_a, select without .lazy) on an unbounded enumerator block forever - only Enumerator::Lazy defers and composes.
Blocks capture their surrounding binding, so a seed held in a mutable local that the block rebinds changes an enumerator that has not converged, and the closure keeps captured objects alive.
